title: Why it's never too early to start with sales · hancrafted
description: Why early-stage founders should start sales long before revenue is needed, and the first concrete steps to build a sales pipeline.

slides.text: Why it's never too early to start with sales Revenue arrives months after the costs that create it. Find your zero-cash month, then start the sales pipeline before you need the money.
Why watching cashflow is mission critical A good deal can still arrive on a bad date: work backwards from when cash must reach the account.

Watch your cashflow In this fictional example, cash reaches $0 in February, so March's $50,000 payment goes unfunded before April's $1,000,000 receipt arrives. Fictional example · cash received, not booked revenue ( öffnet Sprechernotiz ) January Opening cash $100,000 Cash costs $50,000 Receipts $0 Closing cash $50,000 February Zero-cash month Opening cash $50,000 Cash costs $50,000 Receipts $0 Closing cash $0 March Cash costs $50,000 Cannot fund $50,000 payment April Cash costs $50,000 Customer receipt $1,000,000 Too late without bridge funding Closing cash = opening cash + receipts − payments ( öffnet Sprechernotiz ) Bankrupt Scenario shorthand: unable to pay March's costs If funded: March −$50,000; April $900,000
Why sales is more than just selling

Sales is more than selling Three questions to work on together, not three proven causes of trust. Market insight test a real offer ( öffnet Sprechernotiz ) Customer trust earn reasons to continue ( öffnet Sprechernotiz ) Internal insight test your promises ( öffnet Sprechernotiz ) Increase trust? A possibility to earn, not an automatic result of outreach ( öffnet Sprechernotiz ) Learn before you depend on the cash

Stages of sale A lead becomes an opportunity only when the buyer responds, fits and agrees a next step. The work after that decides the deal, and won is not cash received. Leads Research and maintain a prospect list Company and the relevant role Your problem hypothesis Where you found it How you could reach someone Contact status and next action Update the entry after every response Sample list card · fictional Alder Works operations buyer manual scheduling problem source: trade directory contact route: introduction status: not contacted Make first contact A plausible reason and a suitable route? Use it Cold call · inbound enquiry · network introduction Open with the problem you want to discuss Ask for one next step Qualify ( öffnet Sprechernotiz ) Buyer response + plausible fit + agreed next step First contact alone does not cross it Opportunities Agreed problem and next conversation Follow-up Meetings Proposal Negotiation Every step ends with a next action and a date Fictional: Birch Studio described a scheduling problem and agreed to discuss a trial Closing Won: agreement Lost: record reason ( öffnet Sprechernotiz ) Won is not cash received

Stages of after-sale Agreement starts delivery work. Payment arrives when the agreed terms say, and repeat business needs its own agreement. Production Do the promised work ( öffnet Sprechernotiz ) Fictional: prepare Birch's scheduling setup and make time to support it Delivery / operations Get it into the customer's hands Fictional: a setup session that agrees who receives it, how the team starts and what counts as delivered Customer success Check the customer's outcome ( öffnet Sprechernotiz ) Fictional: can Birch plan next week's jobs? Where does it still get stuck? Repeat or recurring business, if earned and agreed New opportunity Needs its own agreement, price and payment schedule. Not in next month's cash plan before then Payment follows agreed terms: before, during or after delivery Before delivery During After delivery

Watch your cashflow, revenue pulled in Same deal, same costs: receiving the $1,000,000 in February instead of April funds March. Only the cash date moved. Fictional example · cash received, not booked revenue Counterfactual: customer cash arrives in February; costs unchanged Receipt moved from April to February January Opening cash $100,000 Cash costs $50,000 Receipts $0 Closing cash $50,000 February February: $0 → $1,000,000 Opening cash $50,000 Customer receipt $1,000,000 Moved ( öffnet Sprechernotiz ) from April Cash costs $50,000 Closing cash $1,000,000 March Opening cash $1,000,000 Cash costs $50,000 Receipts $0 Closing cash $950,000 April Opening cash $950,000 Original receipt date ( öffnet Sprechernotiz ) Moved to February Cash costs $50,000 Closing cash $900,000 Closing cash = opening cash + receipts − payments An earlier signature alone changes none of these cash balances
Why building an effective sales pipeline takes time

What is a sales pipeline A pipeline is our working record of potential deals; a funnel counts how many progress. Volume how many enter each stage? Offering / conversion ( öffnet Sprechernotiz ) which advance? Efficiency / cycle how long does progress take? Pipeline: records and next actions Leads Opportunities Won Funnel: how many progress Leads Opportunities Won Define entry, exit, cohort ( öffnet Sprechernotiz ) and dates before comparing numbers

Pipeline by the numbers An invented, completed cohort: the ratios count progress; the time rail adds duration separately. Illustration, not benchmark 27 leads 3 leads : 1 opportunity · 1/3 advance 9 opportunities 9 opportunities : 1 deal · 1/9 advance 1 won deal 27 leads : 1 deal · 1/27 ≈ 3.7% overall One completed cohort; every successful path passes both gates in order Lead work: 2 weeks Opportunity work: 6 months Closing: 3 months About 9.5 months, counting 2 weeks as about half a month Illustrative sequential first-contact-to-win path, not time to cash receipt Cash timing also needs delivery and payment terms

Pipeline tools in practice Track your deals in a simple pipeline. Example records, not a product screenshot Leads Alder Works Not contacted · owner: founder · next: request introduction, 6 Jan Opportunities Birch Studio Problem confirmed · next: scope meeting, 10 Jan Closing Cedar Labs Proposal discussed · next: payment-terms review, 14 Jan Won Delta Office Agreed 5 Jan · receipt expected 20 Feb Lost Elm Services No current budget · revisit only if timing changes Birch Studio First contact: 3 Jan opportunity entered: 7 Jan last contact: 8 Jan next step: 10 Jan receipt date: not agreed Update after contact review next actions weekly keep open, won and lost separate

How marketing feeds the pipeline Marketing hands a named entry to the pipeline; qualification still decides what becomes an opportunity. Attention Anonymous viewers · outside the pipeline Useful article → enquiry Relevant event → requested follow-up Network introduction → conversation Pipeline Identified lead Buyer response, plausible fit, agreed next step Not qualified / not now Qualified opportunity Birch Studio · scheduling problem · source: article enquiry · owner: founder · next: discovery call More attention is not automatically more deals

Why it takes time to ramp up Separate the sources of delay: they are not three standard durations to add together. Preparation list, offer, stage rules Unknown market test buyer response Unknown metrics wait for outcomes Construct the pipeline Learn the selling work Buyer decision time No measured pipeline-from-zero duration here

Watch your cashflow, "Start when?" Plan backwards from the cash you need, then act forwards. Fictional example · cash received, not booked revenue Start when? Q1 is not a proven latest safe start Start now · before you need the cash First contact Opportunities Closing Planned April receipt Q1: January–March; Q2: April Q1 Q2 January Opening cash $100,000 Cash costs $50,000 Receipts $0 Closing cash $50,000 February Zero-cash month Opening cash $50,000 Cash costs $50,000 Receipts $0 Closing cash $0 March Cash costs $50,000 Cannot fund $50,000 payment April Cash costs $50,000 Customer receipt $1,000,000 Too late without bridge funding Closing cash = opening cash + receipts − payments February receipt would change the outcome 1 Find your zero-cash month 2 Research and maintain a prospect list 3 Make first contact 4 Track stages, conversion and cycle

Why watching cashflow is mission critical Keine Sprechernotizen für diese Folie.

Watch your cashflow Recognition has its own trigger IFRS 15 ties revenue recognition to satisfying a performance obligation through transfer of a good or service. That accounting trigger is not the receipt of cash; the board is deliberately not an income statement 1 . Quellen (1) European Commission, Regulation (EU) 2016/1905 (endorsing IFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers) ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) eur-lex.europa.eu Expenses and payments can differ too Publication 538 distinguishes incurred expenses under accrual accounting from paid expenses under cash accounting. It describes US tax accounting, not a universal financial-reporting rule; this example explicitly assumes costs are paid monthly 1 . Quellen (1) Internal Revenue Service, Publication 538: Accounting Periods and Methods ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) irs.gov
Why sales is more than just selling Keine Sprechernotizen für diese Folie.

Sales is more than selling Two different intention results Murphy et al.'s stated-preference meta-analysis found a median hypothetical-to-actual willingness-to-pay ratio of 1.35 across 83 observations from 28 studies, with substantial skew. Morwitz et al. found weaker intention–purchase correlation for new than existing products. Neither result gives a correction factor for a B2B prospect or proves that all purchase intentions exaggerate demand 1 2 . Quellen (2) Murphy et al., A Meta-analysis of Hypothetical Bias in Stated Preference Valuation ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) link.springer.com Morwitz, Steckel and Gupta, When do purchase intentions predict sales? ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) doi.org History has counter-evidence Poppo, Zhou and Ryu report that continuity expectations mediate the positive history–trust relationship; with weak continuity expectations, longer history was associated with lower trust. Doney and Cannon found no effect of trust on current supplier selection after controlling for previous experience and performance, although trust related to anticipated future interaction. These abstract-level findings are not proof that early startup outreach causes trust or purchases 1 2 . Quellen (2) Poppo, Zhou and Ryu, Alternative Origins to Interorganizational Trust: An Interdependence Perspective on the Shadow of the Past and the Shadow of the Future ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) doi.org Doney and Cannon, An Examination of the Nature of Trust in Buyer-Seller Relationships ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) doi.org Commitment is not trust Anderson and Weitz studied idiosyncratic investments and commitment in 378 manufacturer–distributor pairs. That is evidence about commitment, not a measurement of trust; these concepts must not be interchanged 1 . Quellen (1) Anderson and Weitz, The Use of Pledges to Build and Sustain Commitment in Distribution Channels ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) doi.org What the internal-learning trial tested Both groups of 116 Italian startups received feedback training; the treatment group additionally learned predictive frameworks and rigorous hypothesis tests, performed better and pivoted more. The trial did not isolate sales contact, measure capacity limits or compare feedback with no feedback 1 . Quellen (1) Camuffo et al., A Scientific Approach to Entrepreneurial Decision Making: Evidence from a Randomized Control Trial ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) doi.org
How to start doing sales Keine Sprechernotizen für diese Folie.

Stages of sale Qualification is a separate transition Dynamics 365 distinguishes a lead record from the opportunity record created through qualification. Budget and a clear decision timeline are its example of qualification evidence, not mandatory criteria imposed here on every startup 1 . Quellen (1) Microsoft, Qualify and convert a lead to opportunity ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) learn.microsoft.com Do not erase disqualified leads Microsoft's model retains a disqualified lead as an audit trail. The simple instructional flow uses that principle without copying a vendor's entire stage model 1 . Quellen (1) Microsoft, Qualify and convert a lead to opportunity ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) learn.microsoft.com

Stages of after-sale Relationship performance is broader than trust Palmatier et al.'s meta-analysis reports relationship-marketing performance effects and stronger effectiveness in certain relationship-relevant settings and with an individual person. It does not establish that a customer-success step automatically creates renewals, nor does its moderator isolate trust 1 . Quellen (1) Palmatier et al., Factors Influencing the Effectiveness of Relationship Marketing: A Meta-Analysis ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) doi.org Doing work by hand can reveal process details Graham's practitioner example describes a hardware startup assembling early watches and learning details such as the importance of sourcing good screws. It is an example about early users and production, not measured evidence of paying-customer retention 1 . Quellen (1) Graham, Do Things that Don't Scale ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) paulgraham.com

Watch your cashflow, revenue pulled in A prepayment reverses the receipt lag IFRS 15 describes a contract liability when a customer pays, or payment becomes due, before transfer of the promised goods or services. Cash can arrive before recognised revenue; an advance payment brings obligations as well as liquidity 1 . Quellen (1) European Commission, Regulation (EU) 2016/1905 (endorsing IFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers) ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) eur-lex.europa.eu Deferred payment carries liquidity risk The EU late-payment directive describes deferred-payment B2B trade and the adverse liquidity effects of late payment. Its contractual-period rules are jurisdiction-specific, not a universal promise about when a customer's invoice will clear 1 . Quellen (1) European Parliament and Council, Directive 2011/7/EU on combating late payment in commercial transactions ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) eur-lex.europa.eu
Why building an effective sales pipeline takes time Keine Sprechernotizen für diese Folie.

What is a sales pipeline Default report populations differ Pipedrive's documented default deal-conversion report uses deals created in a period and marked won or lost, whereas HubSpot's funnel dates filter stage activity. Such reports do not automatically compare the same cohort, especially when open deals remain unresolved 1 2 . Quellen (2) Pipedrive, Insights reports: deal conversion ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) support.pipedrive.com HubSpot, Create custom funnel reports ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) knowledge.hubspot.com Forecast weights are settings HubSpot's default stage probabilities weight deal amounts and can be customised. A configured probability is not an observed stage-to-stage conversion rate and should not be presented as one 1 . Quellen (1) HubSpot, Set up and customize pipelines ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) knowledge.hubspot.com

Pipeline by the numbers Real reports may skip gates HubSpot permits optional funnel stages; Pipedrive counts won deals as completing every stage. Multiplying conditional rates is valid for the worked example's strict same-cohort sequence, not automatically for cumulative reached-stage percentages or arbitrary CRM exports 1 2 . Quellen (2) HubSpot, Create custom funnel reports ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) knowledge.hubspot.com Pipedrive, Insights reports: deal conversion ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) support.pipedrive.com Buying groups vary, without a measured clock Johnston and Bonoma studied 31 firms' capital-equipment and industrial-service buying groups and found differences in group structure and interaction. That supports variation by purchase situation, not a measured duration of the example's stages 1 . Quellen (1) Johnston and Bonoma, The Buying Center: Structure and Interaction Patterns ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) doi.org Public procurement is a bounded special case EU public-procurement open procedures carry an ordinary 35-day tender-receipt minimum, with conditional shortening routes including qualifying prior notice, urgency and electronic submission. Those legal clocks have conditions and are not private-company sales-cycle benchmarks 1 . Quellen (1) European Parliament and Council, Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) eur-lex.europa.eu

Pipeline tools in practice Stage evidence can be made explicit HubSpot's example default pipeline separates appointment, qualification, presentation, decision-maker buy-in and contract-sent evidence. Those names are configurable; the fictional board deliberately uses a smaller instructional set rather than claiming those defaults fit every organisation 1 . Quellen (1) HubSpot, Set up and customize pipelines ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) knowledge.hubspot.com Qualification can leave an audit trail Dynamics 365's documented disqualification retains the lead record. Recording a loss or lack of fit is therefore different from quietly deleting it and losing the denominator 1 . Quellen (1) Microsoft, Qualify and convert a lead to opportunity ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) learn.microsoft.com

How marketing feeds the pipeline Marketing and sales qualification are distinct definitions HubSpot's lifecycle model separately defines Marketing Qualified Lead and Sales Qualified Lead. Its configurable stages describe handoff ownership, not measured causal effects of a marketing channel on sales 1 . Quellen (1) HubSpot, Use lifecycle stages (HubSpot Knowledge Base) ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) knowledge.hubspot.com Entry routes are broader than one funnel Microsoft's documented process includes website opt-ins, email enquiries and trade-show cards as lead sources. These are examples of recorded entry routes, not evidence of a universally best channel or its conversion rate 1 . Quellen (1) Microsoft, Understand the sales process (Dynamics 365 Sales documentation) ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) learn.microsoft.com

Why it takes time to ramp up Tenure is not a stopwatch for ramp-up Peasley and Hochstein's authors' summary discusses early-tenure salespeople hired 18–24 months before the survey; that tenure and their framing do not measure a founder's pipeline-from-zero ramp period. The source also reports a prospecting-versus-account-work trade-off, not that maximum prospecting is always best 1 . Quellen (1) Peasley and Hochstein, Insights for Optimizing Early-Tenure Sales Success (summary of their Journal of Personal Selling & Sales Management article, doi:10.1080/08853134.2024.2316383) ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) kellercenter.hankamer.baylor.edu Training evidence has a narrow setting Chung, Kim and Park fit a structural model to one firm's sales force; tenure and training affected modelled performance, with stronger training effects for junior staff. That does not establish how long a startup founder needs to become productive 1 . Quellen (1) Chung, Kim and Park, The Comprehensive Effects of Sales Force Management: A Dynamic Structural Analysis of Selection, Compensation, and Training ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) hbs.edu Budget association is not a timing prescription The longitudinal B2B high-tech startup survey associates a larger personal-sales budget share with better early-stage performance and worse later-stage performance. It does not demonstrate that a budget shift causes faster ramp-up; this result was available at abstract level 1 . Quellen (1) Vomberg et al., The Different Effects of Mass-Media Marketing and Personal Sales Budgets Across the Life Cycle of B2B High-Tech Start-Ups ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) doi.org Buyer-led journeys are conceptual evidence Kalwey et al.'s interview-based conceptual paper describes a role coordinating buyer–seller touchpoints. It does not quantify sales-cycle duration or prove a combined duration for construction, learning and buyer pacing 1 . Quellen (1) Kalwey et al., Holistic Selling: An Emerging Paradigm in B2B Markets ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) doi.org

Watch your cashflow, "Start when?" An unpaid earned amount is not spendable cash IFRS 15 distinguishes contract assets and receivables after transfer from cash settlement. A receivable can record a right to payment while the account still lacks the funds needed for an outgoing payment 1 . Quellen (1) European Commission, Regulation (EU) 2016/1905 (endorsing IFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers) ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) eur-lex.europa.eu Payment risk is distinct from deal risk The EU directive documents that invoices may be paid after agreed terms, with consequences for liquidity. A cash scenario should therefore allow receipt-date uncertainty even after the sales opportunity has become an agreement 1 . Quellen (1) European Parliament and Council, Directive 2011/7/EU on combating late payment in commercial transactions ( öffnet in neuem Tab ) eur-lex.europa.eu

script.text: Dieses Fenster zeigt die Sprechernotizen und den Sprechtext zur Folie, die Sie gerade lesen, und folgt Ihnen beim Scrollen. Mit Alt+N öffnen und schließen Sie es.

Why watching cashflow is mission critical 0:00 – 0:26 A good deal, a bad date Imagine winning a million-dollar customer and still running out of money. Our fictional company builds scheduling software for small teams. Its big customer pays in April. But the company cannot fund its March bills. The deal sounds wonderful. The date makes it useless for getting through March. How did we get here? 0:26 – 0:52 Work backwards from cash Let us put ourselves in the founders' position. They are building the product. They are paying people. They plan to focus on sales when the product feels ready. Before making that decision, they need a different starting point. When must money reach their account? We will work backwards from that deadline.

Watch your cashflow 0:00 – 0:27 Count January first We give this company one hundred thousand dollars at the start of January. Each month, it pays out fifty thousand dollars. Nothing comes in during January. Subtract fifty thousand from one hundred thousand. January ends with fifty thousand dollars. These are invented numbers. Keep them in mind, because we will return to this company. 0:27 – 0:54 Zero is the warning February starts with the remaining fifty thousand dollars. Another fifty thousand goes out. Now the account is empty. March needs another fifty thousand, but there is nothing to pay it with. April's million does not solve March. In this example, nobody has agreed to lend the missing money. The company has to stop. 0:54 – 1:21 A signature cannot pay payroll Imagine the founder celebrating a signed contract while preparing the next payroll payment. The bank asks for available money, not a signature. So do not stop at the deal date or the revenue figure in your plan. For this decision, ask one plain question. On which date can we actually use the customer's money? 1:21 – 1:46 Build your own monthly view Build a simple month-by-month cashflow view. A spreadsheet is enough. Start each month with its opening cash. Add the customer money you expect to receive that month. Subtract the payments you expect to make. That gives closing cash. Carry it into the next month. Repeat this calculation across the months ahead. 1:46 – 2:12 Mark the zero-cash month Find the first month whose closing cash reaches zero or goes below it. Mark that month. Then try a less comfortable version of your plan. Move an expected receipt back a month. What changes? If the balance gets tight, check the individual payment dates too. A monthly total can hide a difficult week. 2:12 – 2:40 Do not wait for the alarm Our founders can see the March problem while they still have January's money. That is the moment to ask what work must happen before a customer pays. Waiting until the account is empty leaves no room for that work. The cashflow view is not just a warning. It tells us why we need a pipeline.

Why sales is more than just selling 0:00 – 0:27 Use the lead time There is work between deciding to sell and receiving money. We can use that time deliberately. Our scheduling company can speak with potential customers while it is still building. Those conversations need a purpose. We want to test a route to a paying customer, not simply collect friendly conversations and call that sales.

Sales is more than selling 0:00 – 0:28 Test an offer, not applause Suppose our founder offers to help a workshop organise next week's jobs. She names the scheduling problem, proposes a price and asks for a conversation about a small trial. Now she has something concrete to discuss. Does the buyer ask about the trial? Ask about the price? Or decline the conversation? Write down the response. 0:28 – 0:55 Learn from a no A workshop manager might say that scheduling is someone else's responsibility. Another might be interested, but not during its busy season. A third might not understand what would change. These imagined answers suggest different next questions. Ask who owns scheduling, when a discussion would make sense, or which part of the offer was unclear. 0:55 – 1:22 Early buyers are a small sample Our founder starts with two people she already knows. Both enjoy talking about software. Before rebuilding the product around their suggestions, she should speak with other kinds of buyers too. Perhaps a team without a technical enthusiast. Perhaps a team with a different way of scheduling. Compare the responses before making a large commitment. 1:22 – 1:49 Give reasons to keep talking I would give the founder a small promise she can keep. Send the agreed trial outline on Friday. Admit which features are not ready. Arrive prepared for the next conversation. These are practical choices, not a recipe that guarantees trust. The buyer still decides whether to continue. A first message does not settle that decision. 1:49 – 2:18 Test what you can deliver Now imagine the buyer asks for a trial next week. Our founder has to check what that promise would require. Can the team import this workshop's existing schedule? Who will answer questions? Write down what is known and what still needs testing. This is a possible delivery problem to investigate, not proof that the team cannot deliver. 2:18 – 2:45 Turn contact into a learning loop Start with an assumption: a workshop wants help with scheduling. Make a specific offer. Record the response. Choose the next test from that response. If the question was unclear, rewrite it and try again. Do not change everything after every call. The purpose is to make better decisions while pursuing customers who may actually pay.

How to start doing sales 0:00 – 0:27 Make the first moves concrete What should our founder do tomorrow? Find potential customers. Contact one. If a useful conversation opens, work out whether there is a real opportunity. Then do the work needed to reach an agreement. There is work after agreement too. We will follow that route, because the cashflow question remains at the end of it. 0:27 – 0:54 Keep the method small You do not need to build a sales department before taking the first step. You need somewhere to record who you might contact and what you will do next. Keep the first version small enough to use tomorrow. A method that you maintain is more useful here than an elaborate system you never open.

Stages of sale 0:00 – 0:28 Choose who might have the problem Let us introduce two fictional prospects. Alder Works is a workshop. Birch Studio is a small design team. Our founder thinks both might struggle to schedule jobs. At Alder, she wants to reach the person organising workshop operations. At Birch, she wants to find whoever plans the team's work. These are starting hypotheses, not confirmed needs. 0:28 – 0:56 Build and maintain the list Start lead generation now. Research and maintain a list of potential customers. For Alder, record the company name, the relevant role and your scheduling hypothesis. Add where you found it, how you could reach someone, its contact status and your next action. After a response, update the entry. The list should reflect what you know today. 0:56 – 1:23 Research is not contact Our founder could spend all week finding more workshops. But a longer list would not answer whether Alder wants a conversation. Once she has a plausible reason for contact and a suitable route, she should use it. Research prepares the first move. It should not become a way to postpone hearing an answer. 1:23 – 1:51 Make the first contact Make first contact to open a conversation. That could be an appropriate cold call. It could be answering an inbound enquiry. It could be asking someone in your network for an introduction. Our founder chooses an introduction to Alder's operations manager. She explains the scheduling question she wants to discuss, rather than sending her entire product story. 1:51 – 2:20 Ask for one next step Birch has asked about the scheduling offer. Our founder proposes a short conversation about how the team plans jobs today. That is one clear next step. She does not assume Birch wants to buy. She asks whether the conversation would be useful and waits for an answer. The invitation gives the buyer something specific to accept or decline. 2:20 – 2:49 Open an opportunity with evidence For this example, our founder sets a simple rule. She opens an opportunity when a conversation reveals plausible fit and the buyer agrees to a next step. Birch describes a scheduling problem and agrees to discuss a trial. That gives her work to pursue. Alder has not replied yet. She cannot treat that silence as an active deal. 2:49 – 3:26 Work opportunities deliberately This is where the real work sits. With Birch, our founder must understand the problem, arrange the scope meeting and answer practical questions. She may need to revise a proposal or negotiate what is included. Each conversation ends with a next action and date. Follow up on that action. Record whether the deal is won or lost. Do not just move a card and wait for money. Agreement still needs its own payment plan.

Stages of after-sale 0:00 – 0:27 A win starts another responsibility Suppose Birch agrees to the trial. Now our company has a promise to fulfil. Someone must prepare the scheduling setup. Someone must make time to support it. The founder puts those tasks into the work plan and their payments into the cash plan. Signing the trial does not switch off the company's monthly bills. 0:27 – 0:54 Delivery must reach the buyer A finished setup on our founder's laptop is not yet a handoff to Birch. They need to agree who receives it, how the team starts using it and what counts as the promised delivery. In this fictional trial, the founder arranges a setup session. Another offer might need a different handoff. Name the responsibilities. 0:54 – 1:21 Ask whether the outcome happened After the trial begins, ask Birch what happened to the scheduling problem. Can the team plan next week's jobs? Where does it still get stuck? If nobody is using the setup, find out why before proposing more work. The next conversation is about the customer's result, not just whether our team completed its task. 1:21 – 1:49 Recurring is conditional Our founder can ask whether Birch wants another project or an ongoing arrangement. Put that possible work back into a new opportunity. Do not put money into next month's plan just because the trial went well. Any repeat purchase needs an agreement. Specify its price and payment schedule instead of assuming the first agreement covers it.

Watch your cashflow, revenue pulled in 0:00 – 0:27 Move cash, not the signature Return to our company with one hundred thousand dollars at the start of January. Let us change one assumption. Instead of receiving the million in April, suppose it receives the money in February. This is an alternative story, not a prediction. The monthly payments stay at fifty thousand dollars. Only the receipt date moves. 0:27 – 0:55 Check February's arithmetic January still ends with fifty thousand dollars. February starts there, adds one million and pays out fifty thousand. It closes with one million dollars. March's payment leaves nine hundred and fifty thousand. April's payment leaves nine hundred thousand. In this version, March is funded. Moving the receipt changes the result without changing the deal's size. 0:55 – 1:23 Ask what could make receipt earlier What would have to change for that version to happen? Our founder would need to discuss timing with the buyer. When could a decision happen? What work must be delivered? Which payment arrangement would both sides accept? Starting sales earlier creates time to explore those questions. It does not give the founder control over the buyer's answer. 1:23 – 1:50 Keep the backup question open The founder should still ask what happens if this earlier receipt is not available. Could the company reduce its planned payments? Would anyone agree to provide bridge funding? Those options need their own work and decisions. Keep the original unfunded case visible. A sales conversation is not a replacement for an emergency funding plan. 1:50 – 2:17 Find the work before the payment Now walk backwards from the required receipt. What must happen after agreement? What must be settled to close? Which questions need opportunity work? Which first conversation could open that work? Which prospects must we research to get that conversation? This chain gives the founder a starting point long before she needs the money.

Why building an effective sales pipeline takes time 0:00 – 0:27 Timing needs a system One promising customer is not enough to tell our founder how her selling works. She needs to repeat the steps and keep records. Which conversations advance? Which stop? How much time passes before an agreement? A pipeline makes that work visible. Over time, those records can help her replace guesses with her own numbers. 0:27 – 0:56 Illustrations are not forecasts We will use a small invented example to understand the numbers. It has a conversion rate and a duration. Neither describes what your company should expect. Think of it as practice with the calculation. When you make your own cash plan, use evidence from your selling work and be explicit about what you still do not know.

What is a sales pipeline 0:00 – 0:27 Records, not a wish list A pipeline is our working record of potential deals. For each one, write its name, current stage, owner and dated next action. Birch is an opportunity with a scope meeting ahead. Alder still needs contact. Those entries tell the founder what to do. A wish that both companies will buy tells her very little. 0:27 – 0:53 Count the flow A funnel answers a different question. How many entered, and how many progressed? Count the researched leads. Then count which became opportunities and which became wins. Keep those categories clear. Adding ten names to the prospect list is more starting volume. It is not the same as opening ten opportunities with buyers. 0:53 – 1:19 Measure conversion with a denominator To measure conversion, divide the number that advanced by the number that entered. Say how many you started with. Follow that same starting group through the stages. For overall conversion, divide its wins by its original leads. If some are still open, show them separately. We cannot yet describe their final outcomes. 1:19 – 1:46 Conversion raises questions about the offer Suppose few of our founder's conversations move forward. She can examine the response notes. Did she reach people with the scheduling problem? Was her invitation clear? Did price become a sticking point? Was this simply the wrong time? The rate tells her where to look. It does not choose the explanation for her. 1:46 – 2:13 Measure the sales cycle explicitly Measure your sales cycle too. Choose a start and an end, then record both dates. In this talk, we use first contact to a won agreement. Count the elapsed time between them. Keep the receipt date in another field. That lets our founder ask both when she reached agreement and when the money became available. 2:13 – 2:42 Efficiency is not speed at any cost If Birch has waited a week for our founder's trial outline, sending it is a useful next action. If Birch needs an internal discussion, another daily reminder may not help. Look at what the elapsed time contains. More prospects, better progression and less avoidable waiting are different questions. Do not answer all three by demanding faster calls.

Pipeline by the numbers 0:00 – 0:27 Read the example as inputs Imagine our scheduling company has finished working through a group of twenty-seven leads. We know the final outcomes for this invented group. Every win in this example went through an opportunity first. Nobody is still waiting for an answer. With those assumptions in place, we can practise counting the route from leads to deals. 0:27 – 0:53 Three leads for one opportunity Nine of the twenty-seven leads became opportunities. Divide nine by twenty-seven. One third advanced. Another way to say it is three leads for each opportunity. That is a relationship between counts. It tells us nothing about how long any conversation took. For timing, we will need a separate set of dates. 0:53 – 1:20 Nine opportunities for one win Of those nine opportunities, one became a won deal. One divided by nine is one ninth. Think about the work behind those nine records. Our founder still had conversations to prepare, questions to answer and proposals to discuss. Only one ended in a win. The other work happened too, even though it produced no agreement. 1:20 – 1:48 Multiply only this consistent path For our invented group, multiply one third by one ninth. The result is one twenty-seventh, or about three point seven percent. We can check it directly: one win from twenty-seven original leads. That describes this completed example. Finding another twenty-seven names tomorrow would not entitle the founder to another win. She still has to do the work. 1:48 – 2:17 Add the time on a different rail Now give one successful path an invented timetable. Two weeks of lead work from first contact. Six months of opportunity work. Three months of closing. Assume those periods happen one after another. Counting two weeks as roughly half a month gives about nine and a half months to agreement. This is a timing illustration, not a forecast. 2:17 – 2:46 The buyer has work too Imagine Birch's contact likes the trial proposal but wants a colleague to review it. Perhaps someone else must agree to the spending. Our founder should ask who needs to be involved and what the next decision requires. These are possible steps in this story. She should discover Birch's actual process rather than assume every buyer follows it. 2:46 – 3:11 The bank deadline comes later in the chain Our nine-and-a-half-month illustration ends at a win. Now place the agreed receipt date beside that endpoint. Does payment happen before delivery, during the work or afterwards? A prepaid arrangement would not add a waiting period after the win. Use the actual arrangement to connect the deal timetable to the cash plan.

Pipeline tools in practice 0:00 – 0:28 Start with a board or spreadsheet Track your deals in a simple pipeline. You can begin with a board or spreadsheet you already have. Give it stages for leads, opportunities and closing, plus won and lost outcomes. Add the names we introduced earlier: Alder Works and Birch Studio. The point is to organise the work, not to buy software before starting. 0:28 – 0:56 Give each card a next action Our founder owns both records. For Alder, her next action is to request an introduction on the sixth of January. For Birch, it is a scope meeting on the tenth. Those are different tasks at different stages. At the review, ask what actually happened and what the buyer agreed next. Update the cards from those answers. 0:56 – 1:24 Keep dates for measurement Birch's first contact was on the third of January. It entered the opportunity stage on the seventh. Record later stage changes and the eventual win or loss date too. Add expected and actual receipt dates when known. If no payment date has been agreed, leave it unknown. An empty field is more honest than an invented date. 1:24 – 1:53 Review stuck work Set aside time each week to review the next actions. Did the scope meeting happen? Are we waiting for the buyer, or did we forget our task? Has a buyer explained why the discussion stopped? Use the answers to decide what happens next. Do not assign a comforting chance of winning just because a card has sat there. 1:53 – 2:19 Measure without hiding open deals When reviewing conversion, return to the same group you started with. Count how many reached each stage. Show those still open alongside the final outcomes. For won deals, calculate first-contact-to-win durations. If only one has finished, say so. That is a beginning of evidence, not a stable answer for every future deal. 2:19 – 2:47 Maintain the source list too The board also reminds our founder to keep researching. Alder's contact information might be stale. Another workshop might fit the offer better. Update the source list as you learn. Then choose the next real contact. Do not let maintaining records become the entire activity. The records should help you decide which conversation to pursue next.

How marketing feeds the pipeline 0:00 – 0:28 Attention needs an entry route Suppose our founder writes about the scheduling problem. Someone reads it, but she does not know who. That person is not yet a named entry she can work with. Include a relevant invitation to discuss the problem. Birch sends an enquiry through it. Now she has someone to answer, rather than just a readership count. 0:28 – 0:56 Choose where marketing hands over For our small company, that enquiry becomes a lead for the founder to handle. Decide what information the handoff must contain. Which company asked? What problem did it mention? Who will respond, and when? Put the entry into the same working system as the other leads. Otherwise a useful enquiry may simply wait in an inbox. 0:56 – 1:24 Feed the list, then qualify In this story, Birch arrived through the scheduling article. Record that source. If our founder later meets another team at an event, record what follow-up it requested. If a contact makes an introduction, record the reason. Then ask the questions needed for the next step. The route into the conversation does not answer them for us. 1:24 – 1:53 More volume is not a guarantee Imagine a new article brings many enquiries from teams outside the offer's scope. That would give our founder more responses to handle, but not necessarily more useful opportunities. Some might be a fit later. Some might need something else. When comparing sources, examine who came in and what happened next, not only which source produced the largest count. 1:53 – 2:20 Close the feedback loop Suppose several buyers ask whether the software can handle last-minute job changes. Bring that question back to the article and the offer. Could the explanation be clearer? Are we contacting the right teams? Choose a specific change to test. Marketing and sales can share these questions, with the next buyer conversation showing what happens.

Why it takes time to ramp up 0:00 – 0:27 Preparation is real work At the beginning, our founder must create a usable first version. Research a few prospects. Write the offer. Choose a contact route. Decide what evidence opens an opportunity. Set up the board. None of that requires a perfect system. It requires enough preparation to make the first contact and remember what happens afterwards. 0:27 – 0:55 You do not know the market yet She might initially contact a workshop owner and discover that a different person handles scheduling. She can test that new route on the next call. Or a buyer may object to the trial's scope. She can ask which part is unsuitable. These conversations inform her next move. A handful of answers does not describe every potential customer. 0:55 – 1:22 You do not know your numbers yet On the first day, there are no completed deals to measure. A week later, several conversations may still be open. The founder cannot hurry their final outcomes by filling in a spreadsheet. Keep recording what happens. Until there is enough evidence, use explicit scenarios rather than treating our invented conversion rate as her own. 1:22 – 1:50 Separate the sources of delay Ask what kind of waiting you are dealing with. Are you still building the prospect list? Are you learning how to explain the offer? Or is a buyer considering a decision? Those questions point to different actions. They are not three standard durations to add together. Name the unfinished work instead of guessing a universal clock. 1:50 – 2:17 Balance new leads with current work Our founder has one afternoon. She could research Alder, prepare Birch's scope meeting or fulfil a trial promise. All three might matter. Put the dates and responsibilities together before deciding. Do not celebrate a long contact list if the active opportunity goes unanswered. Choose work that moves the actual customer conversations and commitments forward. 2:17 – 2:46 Start learning before cash is urgent Starting now gives the founder time to make contacts, record responses and try the next steps. As agreements become clearer, update the receipt scenarios in the cashflow view. Some answers may be uncomfortable. Better to see them while there are choices to consider. The process does not promise a completion date. Waiting does not provide one either.

Watch your cashflow, "Start when?" 0:00 – 0:28 Return to the unfunded month Return once more to the original company. One hundred thousand dollars at the start. Fifty thousand paid each month. January ends with fifty thousand. February ends with zero. March cannot be funded. The million is still in April. We have not fixed that story by discussing sales. We have identified the work the founder postponed. 0:28 – 0:55 Plan backwards, act forwards Plan backwards from the cash you need. Ask what delivery and payment arrangement would support it. Ask what decision must come before that work. Ask which opportunity conversations would support the decision. Then act forwards: research a plausible customer, make contact and pursue the agreed next step. Start that chain before the cash becomes urgent. 0:55 – 1:22 Do not mix the two illustrations Our January-to-April cash story and our nine-and-a-half-month sales path were separate examples. Do not squeeze the long path into those four months. Starting in January is not a proven rescue for the March gap. The lesson is the direction of planning. Find the deadline, then examine how much unfinished work sits before it. 1:22 – 1:51 Take the cash action now Your first action is to build the monthly cashflow view and find your zero-cash month. Use your own opening balance, receipts and payments. Write down the month the plan runs out. Try the plan without your largest unconfirmed deal too. That gives you a concrete cash deadline to work with, rather than a general feeling that sales can wait. 1:51 – 2:18 Take the customer actions now Your next actions are to research and maintain a prospect list, then make first contact. Choose a plausible buyer and a suitable cold, inbound or network route. Ask for one useful next step. If a conversation opens, do the opportunity work. A list alone will not prepare the proposal or answer the buyer's questions. 2:18 – 2:48 Keep evidence as you go Finally, track deals in a simple pipeline. Keep dates, next actions and outcomes. Measure conversion with a clear starting count. Measure the sales cycle with clear endpoints. Use what you learn to adjust your plan. You do not need all the answers before the first contact. You need to start finding them now, before you depend on the money.
